item.title: Trump pushed to reinstate Nvidia's CEO while owning millions in company stock
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump holds tens of millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, giving him a personal stake in the company's stock market roller coaster ride over the past two weeks, financial disclosure documents show. Mr. Trump stood to lose large sums with CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt departure, and stood to profit handsomely after he successfully pressed the chip developer's board to reinstate Huang. Nvidia stock surged more than 30% when Huang returned to the company on Monday, reversing a weekslong slide. Huang resigned two weeks ago over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who ran a company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China, and another alleged affair with a subordinate. Mr. Trump said Monday he personally spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced them" to rehire Huang, offering an "assurance" that there was no national security threat. Mr. Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock in his investment accounts as of the end of 2025, according to financial disclosures filed with the Office of Government Ethics. He bought or sold the company's stock in more than 100 transactions that were worth between $27 million and nearly $98 million between January 2025 and September 2026. The value of the president's Nvidia shares increased anywhere from $1.3 million to $14.8 million on Monday, before paring back some of those gains when Nvidia's share price ticked down Tuesday. The range is so large because it isn't clear how many shares of Nvidia the president currently owns, but it can be roughly estimated based on his sales and purchases this year. "President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions," a White House spokesman told CBS News Tuesday, adding that his investments mirror indexes like the Schwab 1000. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers." In addition to the president, several of his appointees to positions in the State, Commerce and Treasury departments as well as the IRS reported millions in Nvidia stock in their investment portfolios. Many have since sold their holdings. Forbes estimates Mr. Trump's net worth at more than $6 billion, making Nvidia a small part of his total wealth. And Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable public companies, at more than $3.7 trillion, so many investors hold shares in the tech giant. Still, some ethics experts questioned Mr. Trump's large stake in Nvidia, especially after he intervened to boost the company's fortunes. "This goes beyond a conflict of interest," said Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "He is squarely, explicitly using his power as president to benefit himself financially. He has prioritized his finances over the security of the nation." Donald Sherman, president of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit government watchdog, told CBS News that Mr. Trump's "continued ownership of stock in this company is the clearest example of how the president's personal financial interest makes everything he does suspect." Mr. Trump's personal investments have drawn controversy in the past, including his stakes in publicly traded energy companies, firms that have business with the government and his family's cryptocurrency firm . He has denied any conflict of interest. Some critics called for legal reforms to prohibit the president and members of Congress from buying and selling stocks while they hold office. Elected officials are generally allowed to trade individual stocks, though lawmakers from both parties have called for the practice to be banned. Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and former chief ethics attorney for the White House between 2005 and 2007, said he has long argued for changes to the federal conflict of interest law that prohibits government employees from participating in matters that result in their personal enrichment while in office. That current law does not apply to the president, vice president or members of Congress, he said. "We need a prohibition on this right away," he said, adding that the new Congress may take up the cause in January. Painter called Mr. Trump's intervention with the Nvidia board "a huge conflict of interest" and overreach of government power. "It's not the job of the government to call up and say who the CEO of a company should be," he told CBS News. The president has defended his decision to intervene , saying on CNBC that "we have to protect our geniuses" and arguing that Nvidia — as the world's leading designer of advanced chips — plays a key role in maintaining the U.S.' lead over China in AI technology. Mr. Trump has also frequently pointed to the performance of the stock market as a barometer of his success as president. Shortly after Huang was reinstated, Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal the "response from the market has been very positive," and "that really shows the decision was right." Beyond Mr. Trump, numerous political appointees held Nvidia stock. Some divested themselves of their holdings after they were appointed to government positions, federal filings show. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin owned between $250,000 and $500,000 in Nvidia stock in March 2026, and sold $500,000 to $1 million in shares of the tech company in June of this year, his financial disclosures show. "As Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin acts to ensure full compliance with all ethics and conflict of interest rules," said a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security. In the Commerce Department, where Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing scrutiny over whether he has done enough to crack down on highly sensitive AI chip sales to China, a number of senior advisers last year reported selling large positions in Nvidia. Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm that was previously run by Lutnick and is now controlled by his sons, reported holding roughly 1 million shares of Nvidia for its clients as of Sept. 30, worth around $228 million at the time. Those shares were worth just over $150 million at Tuesday's price. None of Lutnick's personal financial disclosures filed by the federal government mention Nvidia holdings or transactions. In the State Department, some of Mr. Trump's diplomatic appointees had Nvidia holdings. Charles Kushner, the U.S. ambassador to France and father of Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, reported Nvidia holdings totaling between $1.5 million and $6 million, according to public disclosures filed January 2025. U.S. Ambassador to Costa Rica Melinda Hildebrand reported Nvidia holdings between $5 million and $25 million, her April 2025 disclosures show. The Texas billionaire, who was a major Trump campaign fundraiser, sold the stock in November of that same year, filings show. Warren Stephens, another major Trump donor and ambassador to the United Kingdom, reported Nvidia holdings between $750,000 and $1.5 million, according to his January 2025 disclosures. He sold those shares in July and August 2025, a few months after he was sworn in as ambassador. In the Treasury Department, when she was nominated to be under secretary for International Affairs, Erin Browne held Nvidia shares totaling between $250,000 and $500,000, her disclosures from January show. Browne sold the stock before her confirmation in August, filings show. Todd Newnam, who was appointed chief financial officer of the IRS in January, holds between $115,000 and $250,000 in Nvidia stock, according to his financial disclosure, filed in April of last year. Newnam, a former CEO of a tech company, was part of the Department of Government Efficiency team that sought to streamline government spending and cut the federal workforce. "All OGE (Office of Government Ethics) 278 filers are required to disclose any equity positions they hold and are advised of their recusal obligations in accordance with the ethics rules," an IRS spokesperson said Tuesday, referring to the financial disclosure required by members of the executive branch of the federal government. Many other officials could be indirectly exposed to Nvidia stock if they invested in mutual funds or similar assets. For example, Vice President JD Vance reported $1 million to $5 million in a fund that tracks the S&P 500 — and Nvidia is one of that index's largest components. item.title: Trump’s new tariff plan would bring back much of what the Supreme Court struck down
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new wave of tariffs from the White House would move overall rates almost exactly back to where they stood in early 2026, according to one initial analysis of the new duties. The Yale Budget Lab says the newly unveiled plans , if enacted, would return the US to rates seen just before the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's blanket tariffs in February. Read more: 5 ways to tariff-proof your finances The estimated overall average statutory rate would rise from the current 11.4% to 13.9% early next year. The rate in February, just before the high court struck down Trump's tariffs enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 (IEEPA), was 13.8%. That remains well below the overall rates seen in 2025. The group estimates that 2025 rates exceeded 15%, peaking at nearly 23% in the weeks after "Liberation Day" in April 2025. "The administration said it wanted to rebuild the IEEPA tariff regime using Section 301; with this proposal, it will have done so in the aggregate," the group said in its analysis. The mix of countries bearing the duties will shift slightly, the budget lab noted, with apparel, electronics, and appliances among the biggest categories affected by the new duties. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday. (Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images) Anadolu via Getty Images The reaction from other corners, meanwhile, was that a combination of widespread exemptions, smaller rate changes on other trading partners, and many tariffs that will not be stacked meant the impact could be smaller. "The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, wrote in an analysis. "The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year," he added, noting that an exact projection from his group will come later on. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer downplayed the macroeconomic effects in a CNBC appearance Wednesday, describing the total changes as moves that "really will just top up a few percentage points." He added that the higher rates on China — the one place where the new tariffs are set to stack on top of other tariffs — are an exception and that the situation for most countries will be less dramatic. A new 'deal rate' for dozens of countries One major trading partner dodged new tariffs this week when it was announced that an investigation in Mexico was still being reviewed. Greer added that recent talks have been going well. Canada was also not subject to this eight-month investigation, which wrapped up this week and covered China, the European Union, and 14 other nations. The visitors' entrance to the U.S. Trade Representative's office is seen in 2024 in Washington. (J. David Ake/Getty Images) J. David Ake via Getty Images China is set for a 20% baseline "deal rate," which could jump to 40% if ongoing talks break down, while other partners will see much more modest changes. Rates on some EU goods will jump from 10% to 15% if the new tariffs on excess structural capacity go forward and replace previous tariffs imposed around the issue of forced labor. Yet the exemption for an array of goods that the EU and others enjoy includes key products such as semiconductors, as well as automobiles, steel, and aluminum, which are subject to a separate tariff authority. Other goods the Trump administration has carved out in recent months, notably certain energy and food products, will also be exempted. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: 'Not a close case': Judge orders FCC to halt review of ABC's broadcast licenses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A judge ordered FCC Chairman Brendan Carr to halt its early review of ABC's broadcasting licenses. A federal judge ordered Wednesday that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) halt its early review of broadcasting licenses of eight ABC stations as part of the agency's intense feud with the Disney-owned network. U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan ruled in favor of ABC, who sued the FCC on First Amendment grounds after the agency announced it was moving up the license renewals of eight stations owned by the network years ahead of schedule. "This is not a close case," AliKhan wrote in the ruling. "Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration," an ABC News spokesperson told Fox News Digital . Disney Sues Fcc Over ‘Retaliatory Campaign Against Abc,’ Seeks To Block Early Renewal Proceedings An ABC News spokesperson called the ruling "important victory for the First Amendment." "While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear," an FCC spokesperson said in a statement. "The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations." Read On The Fox News App FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has called for early renewal of eight ABC-owned stations' licenses in April. The licenses were originally scheduled to be renewed between 2028 and 2031. KFSN-TV in Fresno, KABC-TV in Los Angeles, KGO-TV in San Francisco, WLS-TV in Chicago, WABC-TV in New York, WTVD in North Carolina, WPVI-TV in Philadelphia and KTRK-TV in Houston were the stations named by the FCC. Fcc Boss Brendan Carr Maintains Early Abc License Renewal Is About Dei Probe, Not Jimmy Kimmel Controversy While the FCC maintained the license crackdown was focused on the legality of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) practices, Carr's announcement came as tensions reignited between President Donald Trump and ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. Kimmel had quipped First Lady Melania Trump had the glow of an "expectant widow" on his show, a joke made days before a gunman targeted members of the Trump administration at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner but caught national attention after the assassination attempt. Both the First Lady and President Trump called for ABC to take action against Kimmel at the time. Carr had previously leveled a thinly-veiled threat against Disney last year over controversial remarks Kimmel made about the assassination of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk. 'The View' Eased Up On Political Candidate Bookings Amid Fcc Inquiry, Report Says ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr have had an intense feud during the second Trump administration. The FCC separately launched a probe into ABC's daytime talk show "The View" in an effort to upend its status as a bona fide news program, which exempts the network from abiding by longstanding rules requiring equal time for political candidates. In previous court filings, ABC has claimed that the actions taken by the FCC has had a chilling effect on the network's free speech, pointing to how "The View" has refrained from inviting political candidates onto the show as a result of the crackdown. item.title: The $2 trillion chip rally is unraveling. History offers a warning.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The biggest one-day rescue in stock market history is coming undone. Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, and Wall Street's AI doubts are back with a vengeance. Monday was supposed to be the start of the comeback. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board brought Huang back at the White House's urging a week after chip stocks' worst week since 2001 , and the group added about $2 trillion in a day , a record $950 billion of it from Nvidia alone. The sell-off since has hit the whole sector. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank nearly 8% Tuesday, with Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) down roughly 8% to 11% and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) off about 4%. On Wednesday, the index briefly dropped below last Friday's low, as Nvidia and Micron fell as much as 9% and 13%, before buyers stepped in and cut its loss to less than 1%. The pain spread Wednesday morning, when the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell more than 3% and the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) nearly 5%. Dip buyers pushed both indexes back to small losses by the close, though Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) still finished lower. Yahoo Finance Nvidia got its CEO back, not answers Huang's return settled the question of who runs Nvidia. It didn't answer whether the debt-fueled AI-building boom will pay off, with tech borrowing costs climbing and the Fed still expected to raise rates on Dec. 9. Sherwood News' Luke Kawa doesn't blame any single headline. "I think you can pin it on the sum of all the things that everyone's been pointing to for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang Tuesday. Nvidia's board brought Jensen Huang back as CEO on Monday at the White House's urging. REUTERS/Rick Wilking/File Photo Reuters / REUTERS Washington wants to help. President Trump told the New York Post a pardon for Huang is " always an option , I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Asked about a government stake in Nvidia, he said, "It's probably not too late." "I question what kind of a put it is," GammaRoad Capital Partners chief investment officer Jordan Rizzuto said. "I think it may be a very short-term put." Wednesday's new tariff proposal barely moved futures. History says watch Friday's low Turnaround Tuesday showed up on schedule. The next part of the script leans bearish. In the 20 times since 1993 that the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened a Monday 2% or more higher, it gave back at least half of that gain by Wednesday's close only five times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. SPY was on pace to join them Wednesday morning before a late rebound kept it out. Every one of those fades went on to break the prior Friday's low within three months, most of them within a week. Of the 15 bounces that held up, only a third eventually broke the low in that span. Three of the drops came in the fall of 2008. Yahoo Finance calculations For the S&P 500, that low is about 6,883. The longer-term view is more bullish A year later, SPY was higher after 17 of those 20 big Monday rallies. In 2018, the Fed hiked into a nearly 20% drop and then paused, and stocks hit a record by April. Alfonso Peccatiello of the Macro Compass likes that echo but still sees more pain first, toward 6,500. This Fed isn't in a position to blink . Wednesday's PCE report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed core prices up 3.3% from a year earlier, hotter than expected, making a December rate hike all but certain , with more possible early next year. Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments Chip stocks have given back most of their 2026 gains, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index has fallen below its early 2026 ceiling, marked with the blue line. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving. Advisors Capital Management's Gus Scacco expects Wall Street to wait on Huang's Senate testimony Dec. 3. "We're going to probably be in purgatory here for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang . Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com . item.title: 2nd federal judge blocks Trump's latest bid to restrict birthright citizenship
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A second federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration’s latest attempts to restrict birthright citizenship. U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper of Washington, D.C. ordered a preliminary injunction in a 67-page memorandum opinion , in which he asserted the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment "promises citizenship to practically all children born in the United States.” The judge also said the court will prevent federal authorities from enforcing the president’s August executive orders, which sought to limit the scope of birthright citizenship and combat “birth tourism” — which involves traveling to another country for the primary purpose of giving birth on its soil so the child automatically has citizenship. Cooper added the order also seeks to keep the Trump administration “from taking any other actions to deny or infringe on the citizenship of class members.” “It goes without saying that the public interest is always served by having federal agencies follow the Constitution and federal law,” Cooper, an Obama appointee, wrote. The order came after immigrant’s rights advocacy groups , including the American Civil Liberties Union , filed a lawsuit in September challenging the president’s orders. “The merits in this case are clear-cut,” Cooper's memo read. “The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law.” In September, Maryland U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman also blocked the administration’s efforts via preliminary injunction following a challenge two other immigration rights groups. “This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them,” Boardman, a Biden appointee, wrote. item.title: How the FAA's new Line Up and Wait rules may impact Thanksgiving holiday air travel
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Federal Aviation Administration imposed new standards for its Line Up and Wait airport policy on Tuesday that, though not a significant change, could affect travelers during the busy holiday travel season. Line Up and Wait (LUAW) is a procedure that allows planes preparing for departure from busy airports to taxi into position on the runway while they wait to be cleared for takeoff. It’s designed to make airport departures more efficient by putting planes in position to take off as soon as airspace has been cleared. Under the FAA’s new policy , airports can still use LUAW, but they must designate a watch supervisor whose sole job is to oversee LUAW operations and whose attention cannot be split by other tasks. The new rules change guidance from saying that airports “should” have a dedicated LUAW supervisor to saying that they “must” have one. The FAA said the change is intended to “elevate the safety standard” for LUAW operations by “removing ambiguity” about staffing requirements under the old rules. Will the new rules affect Thanksgiving holiday travel? The impact of the policy change on passengers comes down to staffing. At airports with enough staff to assign one person exclusively to LUAW, the effect will likely be minimal. But airports that may be short-staffed, a chronic problem in recent years, might be unable to use LUAW. That could mean slightly longer waits on the tarmac in some cases. Even minor delays caused by the new LUAW policy could be compounded by potential disruptions from the Thanksgiving travel rush , with 417,000 flights expected to depart during the 9-day holiday travel period and stormy weather forecast for both coasts. The new LUAW rules will also be in place for the December holiday travel season. They are scheduled to expire in June. FAA under scrutiny Though the new policy represents a relatively minor procedural update, it comes at a time when the FAA is under intense scrutiny following the historically disruptive nationwide ground stop that resulted in the cancellation of 18,000 flights earlier this month. That outage, plus a series of smaller technical disruptions in the weeks since, has fueled a sense of “outage anxiety” among holiday travelers. In a recent YouGov poll, 72% of respondents said they were concerned about "flight cancellations or significant delays as a result of further disruptions to U.S. air travel" over the holiday travel season. Nearly a third said the ground stop could potentially lead them to alter their travel plans. The new LUAW rules are not related to the ground stop or other recent disruptions. They were first proposed in early October, more than a month before the ground stop occurred. There were no reports of significant delays related to the new rules on Tuesday, the first day they were in effect and the busiest day of the Thanksgiving travel season. Congress is debating whether to provide the FAA with billions of dollars in additional funding to upgrade its infrastructure and implement other changes to prevent future outages. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has asked for $50 billion , but even lawmakers who support a funding boost for the FAA say the final price tag could be much smaller. The debate could affect LUAW operations at the nation’s airports, depending on whether Congress approves funding to help them address staffing shortages that may limit their ability to assign someone exclusively to LUAW. item.title: Macy's parade has marched through snow and storms. This time, it has to wait.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
With stormy weather bearing down on New York, the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed on Wednesday for the first time in its 100-year history . It will now take place on Saturday instead. But while the event itself had never technically been delayed — until now — bad weather has bedeviled organizers and attendees before. Some of this is just the law of averages. Late November is a relatively rainy period in the Big Apple, with measurable precipitation falling 25% to 30% of the time. It’s also peak season for major coastal storms. This week’s storm — an extratropical cyclone along the East Coast — is expected to bring “strong to damaging wind gusts” and “widespread moderate to locally heavy rainfall,” according to the National Weather Service . Wind maps show that those gusts could hit 40 mph in the morning and peak at more than 50 mph during the afternoon . That’s why this year’s parade has been pushed back: The city’s safety rules stipulate that large balloons — the event’s signature attraction — must be grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts surpass 34 mph. And those wind restrictions stem directly from past problems. In 1993, strong gusts sent a Sonic the Hedgehog balloon careening into a lamppost at Columbus Circle; a piece of the lamp pulled off by the punctured balloon injured a child and an off-duty police officer . Then, in 1997, organizers and city officials learned how bad things can get when giant inflatables encounter 43 mph wind gusts in the valley-like gaps between Manhattan’s high-rises. That year, a six-story Cat in the Hat balloon collided with a lamppost at 72nd Street and Central Park West and sent debris raining to the ground. Metal pieces wound up striking a paradegoer, fracturing her skull and leaving her in a coma for 24 days. Three others were injured as well. Then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani formed a task force in response, and that task force came up with today’s wind rules, among other safety measures. (They also temporarily removed lamppost arms along the parade route.) The woman whose skull was fractured later filed a lawsuit seeking nearly $400 million in damages. The case was settled in 2001 for an undisclosed amount. In 2005, an M&M balloon ripped open when it struck a light pole. Pieces of the pole broke off, causing minor injuries to two spectators. In 2006, paradegoers endured nearly 2 inches of rain; in 2019, wind gusts hit 33 mph, right near the limit. In both cases, balloons were flown closer to the ground. Organizers installed wind measurement devices along the parade route to monitor changing conditions, and the taller, upright balloons were rotated into a horizontal, downward position for safety. The snowiest parade on record occurred in 1989, when more than 4 inches of frozen fluff fell by noon. The coldest came in 2018, with frigid temperatures of 17 degrees Fahrenheit (exacerbated by winds up to 20 mph). But each time, the show went on as scheduled. In fact, before this year, only two things had ever really disrupted the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. One was war: The event was not held from 1942 to 1944, while the U.S. was fighting in World War II. The other was (you guessed it) weather. In 1971, a serious storm pummeled New York City. A little more than an inch of rain fell, along with a dusting of snow. But the wind gusts hit a whopping 63 mph in Central Park . All of the parade’s giant balloons were grounded as a result. item.title: Inside the Trump administration's scramble to avert a chemical crisis in Iowa
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — The chaotic lead-up to Wednesday's detonation of barrels of chemicals at a U.S. Army munitions plant in Iowa that raised contamination fears has prompted questions inside the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. President Trump and other administration officials praised the controlled detonation of about 5 tons of degraded lead azide at the plant in Middletown as having "exceeded expectations," saying maximum mitigation efforts were successfully achieved. "Great job by the Army, and others, in Iowa!!! President DJT," Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social about five hours after the blast took place. But White House officials have expressed frustration in internal conversations that they had to scramble to deal with the crisis. The situation rapidly became a national news story, with complaints from Iowa residents that they had not received sufficient notice about the potential dangers. The Army had known since spring that the lead azide at the plant posed a threat to the public and to the environment, but then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll failed to raise the issue to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or to other senior administration officials, according to several U.S. officials who requested anonymity to speak about a controversial topic. A separate source familiar with the discussions surrounding the ammunition said the Army notified Hegseth's office early on. The notification never reached Hegseth directly, other officials said. The process of coordinating the response was triggered before Driscoll left the administration, two sources said. Driscoll resigned in September amid tensions with Hegseth. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle learned of the stored chemicals and the risks in September, officials told CBS News, but didn't brief superiors. There have been discussions about quietly moving Telle out of the acting role in coming weeks, several sources said. Administration leaders at the most senior levels were taken by surprise when they learned Thursday about the extent of the problem as they flew home from China after Mr. Trump's Asia trip, one U.S. official said. That forced White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to launch an intensive response from Air Force One, involving hours of phone calls, a dozen agencies and nearly every member of the Cabinet. Mr. Trump and other White House officials in post-blast conversations Wednesday were relieved about the results of the detonation and the steps taken from Thursday on to handle the crisis. But Mr. Trump was furious about how the Army had handled the matter in the months before that, three of the sources said. The president's plans to golf Wednesday in West Palm Beach were dashed by rain, and he watched the television coverage of events in Iowa closely, sources told CBS News. There have also been internal administration conversations about the role in this by Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's chief of staff, the sources said. Other officials defended the administration action, saying the dozens of lower-level career officials who knew about the impending danger from the lead azide for months appropriately discussed how to handle it. CBS News reached out to the White House for comment. The Pentagon referred questions to the Army, which has not yet responded to a request for comment. In March, the Army officially notified the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that 68 barrels of potentially unstable chemicals were discovered during a routine inspection at the Iowa plant. Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday that the administration became aware about six months ago "that it was impossible to move it — it was impossible to effectively neutralize it without causing significant danger to the surrounding community." Vance said the administration examined other options. But other U.S. officials said the conclusion was reached only about two months ago that a controlled detonation would be the only safe way to get rid of the chemicals. A private contractor retained by the Pentagon looked into potential disposal processes, two of the sources said. Miller worked on the problem over the weekend before the blast, calling various officials, including Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand on Monday, two sources said. The administration sought to keep the response – and the public blame – bipartisan, one of the sources said. Miller thanked Sand and outgoing Gov. Kim Reynolds "for their cooperation and engagement" shortly after the detonation. Sand and Mr. Trump have exchanged some verbal blows. The Democratic governor-elect said on social media Wednesday the "lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," and called for "immediate transparency." Mr. Trump responded by writing that Sand had "hurt and delayed the process" and should stop trying to "nitpick and issue phony complaints." Earlier in the week, Mr. Trump said the detonation wouldn't move forward unless Sand and an appeals court approved, but warned he would hold Sand responsible "for any and all death or destruction" if he blocked the operation. Sand, who did not have authority over the detonation, responded that the Trump administration should make the decision based on the information available. A federal appeals court on Monday cleared the way for the detonation amid challenges from environmental groups and elected officials about the operation's potential risks to public health. The military ultimately went forward with a controlled blast of the material, rather than letting it further degrade. Maps released Tuesday by the Army noted that the dust cloud may travel as far as 100 miles, but the most potent effects would likely be felt within 30 square miles of the munitions plant. Fifteen minutes after the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitoring stations in the area. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA. The Army said it had taken steps to barricade the concrete bunkers holding the munitions and absorb the toxic dust, including with aqueous foam, which is used to extinguish fuel fires. item.title: Pier collapses, seawalls breached, homes flooded as king tides thrash California
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A wave crashes over a breakwater Wednesday as high surf and tides hit Pacifica, south of San Francisco. (Noah Berger / Associated Press) Coastal California communities were deluged Wednesday by powerful waves and record-breaking high tides, breaching seawalls, flooding some homes and causing a chunk of a pier south of San Francisco to collapse amid 20- to 30-foot waves. The damage was greatest in the coastal town of Pacifica, where relentless waves sent water streaming down several city blocks and collapsed a section of the historic pier. A massive swell of ocean water struck the perpendicular portion of the L-shaped pier, causing the vertical supports to suddenly buckle. King tides — fueled by a historic El Niño , record hot ocean temperatures and strong swells coming from the west — set all-time high tide levels in parts of Southern California, flooding multiple homes in Orange County. “This El Niño is unprecedented with its strength,” said San Mateo County Supervisor Ray Mueller. “For this to be happening when it is a beautiful day on the coastside today, in clear sunshine and no wind, is really significant.” As salt water poured over carefully-lined rows of sandbags and inundated multiple homes in Pacifica — where floodwaters were knee-high on some streets by midday — Mueller told The Times that pumps that were supposed to remove floodwaters were all operational, but overwhelmed by the amount of water coming over the seawall. “They’re having a hard time keeping up with the water that’s coming over,” Mueller said, noting that local officials will need help with the recovery. “We really are going to need resources to shore up this entire area. And frankly, these pumps are going to need to be fixed as well, so that they’re operating better.” Waves pound the Pacifica Municipal Pier after a portion collapsed during high surf and tides in Pacifica on Wednesday. (Noah Berger / Associated Press) The section of the Pacifica pier that collapsed Wednesday had come down in previous storms, Mueller said, so it was “not completely unexpected that that section would come down.” Built in 1973, the pier had most recently been closed in June after crews observed cracks running through the landmark structure. Gov. Gavin Newsom said the damage in Pacifica was “heartbreaking.” “This is a preview of things to come,” Newsom told reporters in San Francisco. “This is anomalous today. This is normal tomorrow. This is what our kids will experience every day, and that’s why it’s so important that we not just situationally address moments like this, but sustainably get under the hood and try to solve some of these things.” While temporary flood barriers are helping coastal areas up and down the state, Newsom said, they would not ultimately be enough. “That’s not the solution to these longer-term trend lines,” he warned. On California’s Central Coast, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office issued a shelter-in-place order Wednesday for Pajaro Dunes resort, a small beachside community, “due to high water levels.” In Stinson Beach in Marin County, evacuation warnings were issued for beachfront homes, while shelter-in-place orders went into effect for neighboring roads. As 24-foot waves slammed into the Point Reyes area, the National Weather Service Bay Area urged residents to exercise caution: “Life-threatening surf, strong rip currents and localized coastal erosion expected,” the agency posted on X. “Remain away from the shoreline — do NOT venture onto jetties, piers or rocks!” Big waves slammed into beachfront buildings on Capitola village, south of Santa Cruz, flooding some streets. And in Monterey County, officials closed multiple beaches, warning in a news release that waves could reach as high as 50 feet. A kayaker crosses a flooded road in Mill Valley, Calif., on Tuesday. (Josh Edelson / AFP / Getty Images) Communities across California have been frantically preparing for coastal flooding for weeks after officials warned that major flooding could inundate the coast on Thanksgiving week, peaking Wednesday and Thursday. As residents worked to fortify homes and businesses with tarps and sandbags, some cities and counties closed beaches, issued evacuation warnings and dispatched crews to inspect stormwater infrastructure, install flood barriers and reinforce seawalls. With California facing more exceptional king tides after Thanksgiving week is over — around Christmas and then Martin Luther King Jr. Day — Mueller said residents should prepare for the possibility of even more intense damage. “Imagine everything we have today, but with a storm system on top of it,” he said. “As soon as we get this cleared out, that is what we start to prepare for, because this was a practice drill for what could come.” Waves crash against the shoreline Wednesday in La Jolla. (Sandy Huffaker / For The Times) In Southern California, high tides brought problems to some communities. In San Diego, preliminary data showed the coastal neighborhood of La Jolla recorded a high tide of 8.11 feet, exceeding the previous record of 7.98 feet set on Oct. 27. Santa Barbara recorded a high tide of 8.21 feet, breaking the old record of 8.04 feet. In Los Angeles, the harbor tide gauge in San Pedro hit 8.19 feet, tying the record set last month. Monterey posted a record sea height of 8.02 feet, breaking the record of 7.95 feet set on Jan. 27, 1983. Despite the immense damage in parts of Northern California, the sea level did not break records in San Francisco, peaking Wednesday at 8.21 feet, just shy of Tuesday’s observation of 8.23 feet. In Orange County, Eric McCoy, Huntington Beach’s fire chief, said that multiple homes flooded in Sunset Beach and crews were assessing damage after high tides of 8.3 feet deluged the coastline. In some areas, he said, water had breached seawalls and docks and boats breached pilings. Still, McCoy told reporters, even though the tides were higher Wednesday than they were in October, the city experienced less damage. Residents had mitigated the flooding, he said, by taking significant measures to protect their homes. The public works department had also taken several steps it had never taken before, such as putting ladders in drains and sandbagging seawalls. Tony Nobles, president of the Sunset Beach Community Assn., agreed that residents had taken “extraordinary measures” to protect their homes. He and other volunteers helped set up sandbag walls for people who couldn’t do it themselves, he said, helping secure 35 homes and five businesses. “They learned a lot in October,” Nobles said. “The houses that were well protected didn’t get wet.” Emergency personnel and city workers carry a pump through floodwaters on Bayview Drive in Sunset Beach on Wednesday. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times) On Wednesday morning, Nobles was picking up a water pump he’d delivered to help a resident pump out water when he got a call on his cellphone from an elderly couple whose home he’d helped protect. The couple has three properties that got water damage in October. “You guys stayed dry, right?” Nobles said, leaning against the tailgate of his pickup truck. “Wonderful.” On Bayview Drive, Gary Scott, 71, was plainly pleased with all the work he had done in recent weeks to fortify his home — especially since his efforts last month did not stop water from seeping into his ground floor and causing extensive damage. Scott spent $10,000 on a retaining wall between his house and a neighbor’s property, and spent days with his son and his son’s friends filling and hauling about 240 sandbags to block off the front side of his property with a wall that was five bags tall. Like the city, Scott had learned from the last major flooding. The bags he’d installed in October weren’t high enough that time, so the water poured through them and flooded the first floor of his home. Water also came in from his next-door neighbor’s property, he said. Even though the first floor remained dry, a musty smell still permeated the air. But this time, the sandbags along the front side of the property — covered in one long, extended piece of plastic — held strong, as did the retaining wall Scott had installed. There was no new flooding. A man walks his dogs as a worker moves sand at Sunset Beach on Wednesday. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times) “Everything held pretty good,” McCoy, Huntington Beach’s fire chief, told reporters. But he noted that the city was getting preliminary estimates that the tides could be even higher Thursday. “We just don’t want to let our guard down,” he said. Forecasters warn that more extreme coastal flooding is possible Thursday in Orange and San Diego counties. Major impacts could also be seen in L.A. and Ventura counties, the Central Coast and the San Francisco Bay Area, and moderate impacts are expected in L.A. County, Santa Barbara County and the Monterey Bay area. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week.
